children-s-edition-of-touching-incidents: S. B. Shaw gathered true stories of prayers answered — rescues, healings, and providences — retold simply for young readers. Meant to build faith in children, these touching tales were read in countless Sunday schools. A gentle book from an age of earnest belief.
doe-osti-3030826-geologic-seawater-air-c: GeoSWAC got Puerto-Rico-assessed, and this DOE text evaluates seawater AC. The pages detail the techno findings. The energy folks get their data. The evaluation was techno-economic. The data were energy. The Pue were evaluation. The AC were seawater.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AgentOswaldFBIJ: FBI releases on Lee Harvey Oswald and the Kennedy assassination make up this file set, gathered under a researcher's filing title in the archive. The FBI's Oswald files run to thousands of pages: reports on his defection to the Soviet Union, his return, his Cuban activities, and the investigation after November 22, 1963. Sets like this one collect the Bureau's releases as they came out, piece by piece. The file is kept as issued, for readers working through the Bureau's paper trail.
nasa-tm-19710015944-voltage-transients-d:
Richard C Bainbridge and James Nestor of the Lewis Research Center wrote this May 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2291. It explains voltage spikes in the speed control circuit of a Brayton cycle alternator. The circuit switched power by phase angle, chopping the waveform. Each fast switch could jolt the output voltage. The team needed the cause before flight use.

They simulated the alternator, control circuit, and spare load on an analog computer. The simulation pinned the spikes on the alternator's own self inductance. Rapidly switching currents fought that inductance and kicked the voltage. A line filter already in the design proved effective. It kept the spikes away from the output terminals.
podcast-joerogan-sp6JkY3d0sw:
Hamilton Morris, a chemist and journalist, talks drugs with Joe Rogan in episode 177 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Morris later hosted Hamilton's Pharmacopeia, a TV series visiting drug cultures around the world. Even in this early talk, his mix of lab knowledge and field stories stands out.

Morris explains what key drugs actually do in the brain and body, in plain language. He shares tales from chemists, users, and makers he had met while reporting. Rogan, a veteran of drug talk, compares notes and stories. The episode blends hard science with the human stories that surround these molecules.
